And he set out to do precisely that. That involved:

  • Kicking out the French troops that were still, 20 years after WW I, occupying the Saar territory of Germany to exploit the mines there (and harass the local population while they were at it)
  • Annexing Austria (by popular referendum, 99.73% for joining)
  • Annexing the Sudetenland, a strip of Czechoslovakia where Germans lived historically
  • Restoring Danzig, and German territories taken by the Polish after WW I, to Germany (or at least negotiating a trade route to connect "mainland" Germany to the now disconnected West Prussia)

These objectives, you are quite right, were not to "defend ourselves from being attacked", but to "take back what was ours and bring our people back to their own nation".

Things started escalating only when Poland, encouraged by Britain's and France's promises to have their back, refused any and all negotiations or compromise. They would not even allow trade routes to West Prussia to help them economically, which wouldn't have cost them anything. Finally, claiming that German civilians were being attacked and brutalized by the Polish, Hitler marched German troops into areas previously owned by Germany and still occupied by Germans. Poland responded by bombing the troops. Hitler responded by declaring war on Poland. Britain and France responded by declaring war on Germany. Etc.

What followed was that Germany made short work of Poland and then turned her attention to France, where French and British troops had gathered on the German border. They were severely whipped and ended up in the whole Dunkirk affair, May-June 1940, which, despite Hollywood's efforts to rewrite history, involved Hitler pulling his troops back instead of finishing off the trapped British troops, and giving them time to evacuate while simultaneously suing for peace (a separate occasion, different from the OP). The peace offer was rejected, and so Germany proceeded to make short work of France and turned her attention to Britain.

Britain, however, despite being beaten back at Dunkirk, was in a much better strategic position, given Germany's strength on land but relative weakness at sea and air combat. Germany controlled a wide strip of land across central Europe, from France to Poland, but most of the coastal areas that Britain had easy access to were still "neutral". This gave Britain many options on where to land and attack (good), and put Germany in a position where they had to be able to react to many difficult to predict possible attack routes (bad). So Germany set out to occupy key neutral coastal countries, like Norway, Denmark and Holland, without actually declaring war on them or attacking unless facing resistance. Some didn't resist at all, others engaged in brief local skirmishes, but quickly submitted to occupation. THIS part WAS a "defend ourselves from being attacked [by Britain]" maneuver.
